danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 2
paragraphs: Den niogtyvende maj forlod Napoleon Dresden, hvor han havde tilbragt tre uger omgivet af et hof, der omfattede fyrster, hertuger, konger og endda en kejser. Inden sin afrejse viste Napoleon nåde mod den kejser, de konger og fyrster, der havde fortjent det, irettesatte de konger og fyrster, han var utilfreds med, forærede perler og diamanter, som var hans egne — det vil sige taget fra andre konger — til kejserinden af Østrig, og efter, som hans historiker fortæller os, ømt at have omfavnet kejserinde Marie Louise — som betragtede ham som sin ægtemand, skønt han havde efterladt en anden hustru i Paris — forlod han hende, bedrøvet over den adskillelse, hun syntes knap at kunne bære. Selvom diplomaterne stadig fast troede på muligheden af fred og arbejdede ivrigt herfor, og selvom kejser Napoleon selv skrev et brev til Alexander, hvori han kaldte ham Monsieur mon frère og oprigtigt forsikrede ham om, at han ikke ønskede krig og altid ville elske og ære ham — tog han dog af sted for at slutte sig til sin hær, og ved hvert ophold gav han nye ordrer om at fremskynde troppernes bevægelse fra vest mod øst. Han rejste i en rejsevogn med seks heste, omgivet af pager, adjudanter og en eskorte, ad vejen til Posen, Thorn, Danzig og Königsberg. Ved hver af disse byer blev han modtaget af tusinder af mennesker med begejstring og entusiasme.

Hæren bevægede sig fra vest mod øst, og forspænd af seks heste bar ham i samme retning. Den tiende juni * indhentede han hæren og tilbragte natten i kvarterer indrettet for ham på en polsk greves gods i Vilkavisski-skoven.
* Gammel tidsregning.
Næste dag overhalede han hæren og kørte i en vogn til Njemen, skiftede til polsk uniform og kørte til flodbredden for at vælge et sted til overgangen.

Da han på den anden side så nogle kosakker (les Cosaques) og de vidtstrakte stepper, i hvis midte den hellige by Moskva (Moscou, la ville sainte) lå, hovedstaden i et rige som det Skytien, Alexander den Store havde marcheret ind i — beordrede Napoleon uventet og i strid med såvel strategiske som diplomatiske hensyn en fremrykning, og næste dag begyndte hans hær at krydse Njemen.

Tidligt om morgenen den tolvte juni trådte han ud af sit telt, der den dag var slået op på den stejle venstre bred af Njemen, og kiggede gennem en kikkert på strømmene af sine tropper, der væltede ud af Vilkavisski-skoven og flød hen over de tre broer, der var kastet over floden. Tropperne, der vidste om kejserens tilstedeværelse, var på udkig efter ham, og da de fik øje på en skikkelse i overfrakke og trekantet hat, der stod adskilt fra sit følge foran sit telt på bakken, kastede de deres huer i vejret og råbte: »Vive l'Empereur!« og den ene efter den anden strømmede de i en uafbrudt strøm ud af den vældige skov, der havde skjult dem, og spredte sig og flød videre og videre over de tre broer til den anden side.

»Nu går vi i kamp. Åh, når han selv tager fat, så brænder det på... ved Gud!... Der er han!... Vive l'Empereur! Så det er Asiens stepper! Det er alligevel et grimt land. Au revoir, Beauché; jeg gemmer det bedste palads i Moskva til dig! Au revoir. Held og lykke!... Så De kejseren? Vive l'Empereur!... preur! — Hvis de gør mig til guvernør af Indien, Gérard, gør jeg dig til minister i Kashmir — det er en aftale. Vive l'Empereur! Hurra! hurra! hurra! Kosakkerne — de slyngler — se, hvordan de render! Vive l'Empereur! Der er han, kan du se ham? Jeg har set ham to gange, lige så tydeligt som jeg ser dig nu. Den lille korporal... Jeg så ham give korset til en af veteranerne... Vive l'Empereur!« lød stemmerne fra mænd, gamle og unge, af de mest forskellige karakterer og samfundsstillinger. På alles ansigter var ét fælles udtryk af glæde over det længe ventede felttogs begyndelse og af henrykkelse og hengivenhed for manden i den grå frakke, der stod på bakken.

Den trettende juni blev en temmelig lille, fintbygget araberhest ført hen til Napoleon. Han steg op og red i galop til en af broerne over Njemen, uafladelig døvet af uophørlige og henrykte tilråb, som han tydeligvis kun tålte, fordi det var umuligt at forbyde soldaterne at udtrykke deres kærlighed til ham ved sådanne råb, men som fulgte ham overalt og forstyrrede ham og distraherede ham fra de militære overvejelser, der havde optaget ham fra det øjeblik, han sluttede sig til hæren. Han red over en af de svajende pontonbroer til den fjerne side, drejede skarpt til venstre og galopperede i retning mod Kovno, forudgået af henrykte, beredne chasseurer fra Garden, der åndeløse af begejstring galopperede foran for at bane vej for ham gennem tropperne. Da han nåede den brede flod Vilija, standsede han nær et regiment polske uhlaner, der var opstillet ved floden.
»Vivat!« råbte polakkerne begejstret, idet de brød rækkerne og pressede sig mod hinanden for at se ham.

Napoleon kiggede op og ned ad floden, steg af og satte sig på en træstamme, der lå på bredden. På et stumt tegn fra ham blev en kikkert rakt ham, som han støttede på ryggen af en lykkelig page, der var kommet løbende, og han stirrede på den modsatte bred. Så fordybede han sig i et kort, der var lagt ud på stammerne. Uden at løfte hovedet sagde han noget, og to af hans adjudanter galopperede af sted til de polske uhlaner.
»Hvad? Hvad sagde han?« hørtes i rækkerne af polske uhlaner, da en af adjudanterne red hen til dem.

Ordren var at finde et vadested og krydse floden. Obersten for de polske uhlaner, en smuk gammel mand, rødmede og famlede med ordene af ophidselse, da han spurgte adjudanten, om han måtte svømme over floden med sine uhlaner i stedet for at lede efter et vadested. I tydelig frygt for at få afslag bad han som en dreng, der beder om lov til at komme op på en hest, om tilladelse til at svømme over floden for kejserens øjne. Adjudanten svarede, at kejseren formentlig ikke ville være utilfreds med denne overdrevne iver.

Så snart adjudanten havde sagt dette, løftede den gamle, overskæggede officer, med lykkeligt ansigt og funklende øjne, sin sabel, råbte »Vivat!« og befalede uhlanerne at følge ham, sporede sin hest og galopperede ud i floden. Han gav sin hest et vredt stød — den var blevet sky under ham — og styrtede ud i vandet mod det dybeste sted, hvor strømmen var stærk. Hundredvis af uhlaner galopperede efter ham. Det var koldt og uhyggeligt i den hurtige strøm midt i floden, og uhlanerne greb fat i hinanden, når de faldt af hestene. Nogle af hestene druknede, og nogle af mændene; de øvrige forsøgte at svømme videre, nogle i sadlen, andre klyngende sig til hestenes manker. De forsøgte at nå den modsatte bred, og skønt der var et vadested en tredjedel mil borte, var de stolte af at svømme og drukne i denne flod for den mands øjne, der sad på træstammen og ikke engang kiggede på, hvad de foretog sig. Da adjudanten vendte tilbage og valgte et passende øjeblik, vovede han at henlede kejserens opmærksomhed på polakkernes hengivenhed for hans person, men den lille mand i den grå frakke rejste sig, tilkaldte Berthier og begyndte at gå frem og tilbage på bredden med ham, mens han gav ham instruktioner og lejlighedsvis kastede et misbilligende blik på de druknende uhlaner, der distraherede hans opmærksomhed.

For ham var det ingen ny overbevisning, at hans tilstedeværelse hvor som helst i verden, fra Afrika til Moskvas stepper, var nok til at forbløffe mennesker og drive dem til vanvittigt selvforglemmelse. Han bad om sin hest og red til sit kvarter.

Omkring fyrre uhlaner druknede i floden, skønt der blev sendt både ud for at hjælpe dem. Flertallet kæmpede sig tilbage til den bred, de var startet fra. Obersten og nogle af hans mænd nåede over og kravlede med besvær op på den modsatte bred. Og så snart de var kommet op, i deres gennemblødte og dryppende klæder, råbte de »Vivat!« og kiggede henrykt på det sted, hvor Napoleon havde været, men hvor han ikke længere var, og i det øjeblik anså de sig selv for lykkelige.

Samme aften, mellem udstedelsen af én ordre om, at de falske russiske pengesedler, der var fremstillet til brug i Rusland, skulle leveres så hurtigt som muligt, og en anden om, at en sachser, hos hvem et brev med oplysninger om ordrerne til den franske hær var fundet, skulle skydes, gav Napoleon også instrukser om, at den polske oberst, der unødvendigt havde styrtet sig i floden, skulle optages i Æreslegionen, som Napoleon selv var overhoved for.
Quos vult perdere dementat.
Dem, (Gud) vil tilintetgøre, slår han med vanvid.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Napoleon left Dresden on the twenty-ninth of May, after three weeks there among a court of princes, dukes, kings, and even an emperor. Before he went, he rewarded the emperor, kings, and princes who deserved it and scolded those he was unhappy with. To the Empress of Austria he gave pearls and diamonds that were his own — that is, ones he had taken from other kings. And, as his historian tells us, he embraced the Empress Marie Louise tenderly. She regarded him as her husband, though he had left another wife in Paris, and she was left grieving by the parting, which she seemed hardly able to bear. The diplomats still firmly believed peace was possible and worked zealously for it, and Napoleon himself wrote Alexander a letter, addressing him as Monsieur mon frère and sincerely assuring him that he did not want war and would always love and honor him. Even so, he set off to join his army, and at every station he issued fresh orders to hurry his troops along from west to east. He rode in a coach and six, with pages, aides-de-camp, and an escort around him, on the road through Posen, Thorn, Danzig, and Königsberg. In every one of these towns, thousands of people greeted him with excitement and enthusiasm.

The army was moving from west to east, and relays of six horses took him the same way. On the tenth of June, * he caught up with the army and spent the night in rooms made ready for him on the estate of a Polish count, in the Vilkavisski forest.
* Old style.
The next day he overtook the army and drove in a carriage to the Niemen. There he changed into a Polish uniform and went down to the riverbank to pick a place for the crossing.

Across the river he saw some Cossacks (les Cosaques) and the wide steppes, with the holy city of Moscow (Moscou, la ville sainte) lying in the midst of them, the capital of a realm like the Scythia that Alexander the Great had marched into. Suddenly, against every strategic and diplomatic consideration, Napoleon ordered the advance, and the next day his army began crossing the Niemen.

Early on the morning of the twelfth of June he stepped out of his tent, pitched that day on the steep left bank of the Niemen, and watched through a spyglass as his troops streamed out of the Vilkavisski forest and poured across the three bridges built over the river. The troops knew the Emperor was there and were looking for him. When they spotted a figure in an overcoat and cocked hat, standing in front of his tent on the hill apart from his suite, they threw their caps in the air and shouted, "Vive l'Empereur!" Regiment after regiment came out in an endless stream from the huge forest that had hidden them, then split apart and flowed on and on across the three bridges to the other side.

"Now we'll go into action. Oh, when he takes it in hand himself, things get hot... by heaven!... There he is!... Vive l'Empereur! So these are the steppes of Asia! It's a nasty country all the same. Au revoir, Beauché; I'll keep the best palace in Moscow for you! Au revoir. Good luck!... Did you see the Emperor? Vive l'Empereur!... preur!—If they make me Governor of India, Gérard, I'll make you Minister of Kashmir — that's settled. Vive l'Empereur! Hurrah! hurrah! hurrah! The Cossacks — those rascals — see how they run! Vive l'Empereur! There he is, do you see him? I've seen him twice, as I see you now. The little corporal... I saw him give the cross to one of the veterans.... Vive l'Empereur!" So called the voices of men young and old, of every sort of character and social standing. Every face wore the same look: joy that the long-awaited campaign was beginning, and rapture and devotion toward the man in the gray coat on the hill.

On the thirteenth of June they brought Napoleon a rather small, thoroughbred Arab horse. He mounted and galloped to one of the bridges over the Niemen. The rapturous cheering never stopped and deafened him. Evidently he put up with it only because he couldn't forbid the soldiers to show their love by shouting, but it followed him everywhere, it disturbed him, and it pulled him away from the military concerns that had occupied him since he joined the army. He crossed one of the swaying pontoon bridges to the far side, turned sharply left, and galloped toward Kovno. Mounted chasseurs of the Guard rode ahead of him, breathless with delight and enraptured, clearing a path for him through the troops. At the broad river Viliya he stopped beside a regiment of Polish Uhlans posted on the bank.
"Vivat!" cried the Poles in ecstasy, breaking ranks and jostling one another to see him.

Napoleon looked up and down the river, got off his horse, and sat on a log lying on the bank. He made a silent sign and someone handed him a telescope. He rested it on the back of a happy page who had run up, and gazed at the opposite bank. Then he bent over a map spread on the logs. Without raising his head he said something, and two of his aides-de-camp galloped off toward the Polish Uhlans.
"What? What did he say?" was heard in the ranks of the Polish Uhlans as one of the aides-de-camp rode up.

The order was to find a ford and cross the river. The colonel of the Polish Uhlans, a handsome old man, turned red and, tripping over his words in his excitement, asked the aide-de-camp if he might swim the river with his Uhlans instead of looking for a ford. He was obviously afraid of being refused, like a boy asking leave to mount a horse, and he begged to be allowed to swim across before the Emperor's eyes. The aide-de-camp answered that the Emperor would probably not be displeased by such excess of zeal.

Hardly had the aide-de-camp said this when the old mustached officer, his face happy and his eyes sparkling, raised his saber and shouted "Vivat!" He ordered the Uhlans to follow, spurred his horse, and galloped into the river. His horse had grown restive under him, and he thrust at it angrily and plunged into the water, heading for the deepest place, where the current ran fast. Hundreds of Uhlans galloped in behind him. Out in the middle of the stream, in the rushing current, it was cold and eerie, and the Uhlans clutched at one another as they fell from their horses. Some horses drowned, and some men. The rest tried to swim on, some still in the saddle, some hanging onto their horses' manes. They struggled toward the opposite bank, and though there was a ford a third of a mile away, they were proud to be swimming and drowning in this river under the eyes of the man sitting on the log, who wasn't even looking at what they were doing. The aide-de-camp came back and, picking a good moment, ventured to point out to the Emperor how devoted the Poles were to him. The little man in the gray overcoat stood up, called Berthier, and began pacing the bank with him, giving him instructions and now and then glancing with disapproval at the drowning Uhlans, who were distracting him.

It was nothing new to him to believe that his presence anywhere in the world, from Africa to the steppes of Muscovy alike, was enough to stun people and drive them to mad self-forgetfulness. He called for his horse and rode back to his quarters.

About forty Uhlans drowned in the river, although boats were sent to help them. Most struggled back to the bank they had left. The colonel and some of his men reached the far side and clambered out with difficulty. And as soon as they were out, in their soaked, streaming clothes, they shouted "Vivat!" and looked ecstatically at the place where Napoleon had been, though he was no longer there, and at that moment thought themselves happy.

That evening Napoleon gave one order that the forged Russian paper money, prepared for use in Russia, should be delivered as quickly as possible, and another that a Saxon should be shot, in whose possession a letter had been found with information about the orders to the French army. Between the two, he also gave instructions that the Polish colonel who had plunged into the river for no reason should be enrolled in the Légion d'honneur, of which Napoleon himself was the head.
Quos vult perdere dementat. *
* Those whom (God) wishes to destroy he drives mad.
